source.title: Training Bilingual LMs with Data Constraints in the Targeted Language
source.authors: Skyler Seto; Maartje ter Hoeve; He Bai; Natalie Schluter; D. Grangier

record.file_problem: The full paper is present and readable; there are a few minor text-extraction typos.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests downstream performance across data and model scales, using zero-shot task accuracy rather than the held-out-loss power-law measurements in the claim.
record.gate_note: The scaling-related results are in §5 and Appendices F–G. Other dataset filtering, language, and translation comparisons are not rows here because they do not test downstream predictability with scale. The paper cites scaling laws as motivation; those citations are not treated as results.
record.test_reason: In a bilingual, target-data-constrained pretraining setting, the study reports downstream zero-shot accuracy at several data sizes (0.1B–100B target tokens) and model sizes (300M, 1.3B, 2.7B). This is weak evidence on V6 only: two or three sizes, no fitted law, and no loss-to-task mapping.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right, with two refinements. The authors find that high-quality auxiliary English data (via filtering and topic upsampling) improves target-language performance, mainly for languages close to English, and not for Chinese, Japanese or Korean. They also find that model scaling is limited when target data is scarce: the 2.7B model needs at least about 1B target tokens to gain, and they argue data should scale with model size.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines bilingual data and model scaling using downstream zero-shot accuracy, not held-out-loss power-law fitting or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream gains from model-size scaling depend on the amount of target-language data; accuracy plateaus as data increases. The paper also reports that trends differ across target languages, but those comparisons are not scaling-law tests.

fits_no_version.finding: Validation perplexity for the 2.7B model shows clear overfitting from about 25% of training with 5% repeated target data, while the 1.3B model shows little overfitting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under heavy repetition of scarce data, larger models overfit earlier, so loss gains from parameter scaling vanish (data-constrained scaling).

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (2024)
record.problems: The scaling results relevant here are mostly described qualitatively in the text or figures, without exact plotted values or stated uncertainty. The model-size comparison covers 1.3B and approximately 2.7B parameters, and the non-English evaluations use translated benchmarks.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant scaling results were omitted.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of held-out loss. Perplexity is reported only for overfitting diagnostics (Fig. 15) and for translation familiarity (Table 2).
No compute-optimal allocation. The paper cites Kaplan/Chinchilla only as motivation for data scaling with model size.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
Repeated-data effects appear only as a downstream plateau, with no power-law form tested. Only text modality is studied.
Predictability as a fitted trend, and prediction of downstream accuracy from pretraining loss, are not tested. Only 2–3 model sizes and qualitative data-size curves are reported.
No fitting choices or exponents are compared.

missing.what: 300M vs 1.3B downstream accuracy for the same data recipes. German averages: e.g. Large DE 44.12 vs 48.21, Small DE + FWE 43.75 vs 47.16. English: FWE 52.82 vs 62.05.
1.3B vs 2.7B under different target-data ratios: about equal for 1.3B, while 2.7B is worse at a 5% ratio.
2.7B performs slightly worse than 1.3B at 250M target tokens, with clear validation overfitting.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's focus is data mixing, not scaling laws. Its scaling evidence is qualitative and figure-only, with at most three model sizes, so the V6 verdicts are weak. Non-English evaluations use machine-translated benchmarks. The paper misattributes 'Chinchilla scaling laws' to Kaplan et al. 2020.

versions.untested_parts: It reports some validation-perplexity behavior under data-constrained training, but does not test power-law held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute when the other quantities are not bottlenecks.
No small-run power-law fits or predictions of much larger runs are evaluated.
The paper does not find a loss-minimising parameter/token allocation at fixed compute or fit either allocation as a power of compute.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study concerns text pretraining and does not test other modalities, fine-tuning, or transfer regimes as scaling laws.
It reports downstream accuracy across selected data and model scales, but does not test prediction from pretraining loss or fit a general downstream scaling law.
It does not compare fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices, nor fit and assess departures from a single power law.

rows.subject: 1.3B parameter model
rows.operation_detail: Sweep training-dataset size from 0.1B to 100B tokens.

conditions.value: translated German, average over zero-shot benchmark tasks

rows.baseline: Models trained with 5B tokens of German mC4 data
rows.value: Models trained on English mC4 achieve similar performance.
rows.note: The paper describes the comparison in prose; it does not give the plotted accuracy values there.
rows.check: This is a data-equivalence comparison: English mC4 auxiliary data matches about 5B German tokens. It is an exchange rate between data sources, not a measure of whether downstream accuracy improves predictably with scale.

rows.subject: 1.3B parameter model
rows.operation_detail: Sweep training-dataset size from 0.1B to 100B tokens.

conditions.value: translated German, average over zero-shot benchmark tasks

rows.baseline: Around 10B tokens of German mC4 data
rows.value: Around 50B tokens of FineWebEDU matches the performance of 10B tokens of German mC4 data.
rows.note: The paper describes this approximate token equivalence in prose; exact plotted accuracy values are not stated.
rows.check: This is a data-equivalence comparison: about 50B FineWebEDU tokens match 10B German tokens. It does not measure downstream improvement with scale as V6 names it.

rows.subject: 1.3B parameter model
rows.operation_detail: Increase the amount of training data in the dataset-size sweep.

conditions.value: German mC4 and English mC4 or FineWebEDU
translated German, average over zero-shot benchmark tasks

rows.value: The curves plateau quickly at around 10B tokens.
rows.note: The authors report a plateau across the plotted curves; exact values at individual data sizes are not stated in prose.
rows.check: Accuracy rises with target tokens, then plateaus at about 10B tokens, which corresponds to about 10 data repetitions in a 100B-token run. Gains stop under heavy repetition. No baseline value is given; values can only be read from Figure 9.

source_check.problem: The recorded plateau is correct, but the verdict fix misinterprets repetition: training consumes 100B tokens throughout; increasing dataset size beyond about 10B reduces repetitions below about ten, without further accuracy gains.

rows.subject: 2.7B parameter model
rows.operation_detail: Increase model size from 1.3B to 2.7B parameters.
rows.baseline: 1.3B parameter model trained with 250M target-language tokens
rows.value: Scaling from a 1.3B to a 2.7B parameter model shows limited improvement.
rows.note: The prose gives the qualitative comparison, not exact plotted accuracy values.
rows.check: With 250M target tokens, the text reports limited improvement from 1.3B to 2.7B. Appendix F (Fig. 16a) says the 2.7B model performs slightly worse than the 1.3B model, and Fig. 15 shows clear validation overfitting for 2.7B. The row's value understates this.

source_check.problem: The main text's limited-improvement description is accurate, but Appendix F explicitly reports deterioration, requiring reversed rather than absent.

rows.subject: 2.7B parameter model
rows.operation_detail: Increase model size from 1.3B to 2.7B parameters while increasing target-language data.
rows.baseline: 1.3B parameter model trained with 1B target-language tokens
rows.value: Increasing to 1B tokens results in larger improvements when increasing model size to 2.7B; the authors describe the improvement as doubled.
rows.note: The prose reports the qualitative comparison; exact plotted accuracy values are not stated. The figure caption refers to 1B and 3B models, while the main text identifies them as 1.3B and 2.7B.

source_check.locator_found: §5.2, Figure 10; Appendix F, Figure 16b discussion and caption.

relationships.condition: Model scaling when target data is not the bottleneck: 1.3B to 2.7B with 1B German tokens, and 300M to 1.3B at 250M German tokens (text Tables 12–15).
relationships.reason: Larger models score higher downstream. R5 reports doubled improvement at 1B target tokens. Per the text tables, the 1.3B model beats the 300M model on German averages (e.g. FWE 47.16 vs 43.75), which no row captures.
relationships.display_finding: Larger models score higher downstream, with doubled improvement reported at 1B German tokens and German FWE averages of 47.16 for 1.3B versus 43.75 for 300M at 250M German tokens.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Model scaling when target data is not the bottleneck: 1.3B to 2.7B with 1B German tokens, and 300M to 1.3B at 250M German tokens (text Tables 12–15).
source_check.reason: R5 reports larger downstream gains with 1B target tokens. Tables 13 and 15 confirm German FineWebEDU averages of 43.75 and 47.16 for 300M and 1.3B models. These support directional improvement; they do not establish quantitative predictability or eliminate a data bottleneck.

relationships.condition: Data-constrained, heavily repeated target data: 250M German tokens at 2.7B, and target-data sweeps beyond about 10B tokens.
relationships.reason: At 250M target tokens the 2.7B model is no better, or slightly worse, than 1.3B and overfits (R4). Accuracy plateaus at about 10 repetitions (R3). Downstream gains with scale hold only when unique data grows.
relationships.display_finding: With 250M target tokens, the 2.7B model matched or slightly underperformed 1.3B and overfit, while accuracy plateaued after about 10 repetitions.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Data-constrained, heavily repeated target data: 250M German tokens at 2.7B, and target-data sweeps beyond about 10B tokens.
source_check.reason: Split this group: R4 challenges V6 because Appendix F explicitly reports worse accuracy at 2.7B with 250M target tokens; R3 can retain limits_scope for the dataset-size plateau. Beyond 10B unique tokens repetition decreases, so the plateau does not establish that heavy repetition stops gains. R5 also shows model-size gains with unique target data fixed at 1B.
